lessons.title: Radians, degrees and complete rotations
lessons.summary: Connect an angle to an arc-to-radius ratio and keep its units throughout the calculation.
lessons.objective: Use radian measure, convert exactly between degrees and radians and identify the required angle in a diagram.
lessons.before: Recall angles in triangles and around a point, exact fractions of a turn and basic trigonometry.
lessons.ideas:
One radian is defined by an arc

An angle of one radian subtends an arc equal in length to the radius. More generally, \(\theta=s/r\), when s and r use the same length unit. Radian measure is a ratio; it does not depend on the size of the circle.

Convert through a half-turn

\[\pi\text{ radians}=180^\circ,\qquad \theta_{\rm rad}=\theta_{\rm deg}\frac{\pi}{180}.\]

To convert radians to degrees, multiply by \(180/\pi\). Keep exact multiples of π where possible. A full turn is 2π radians and a right angle is π/2 radians.

Identify the intended angle

Angles in a triangle sum to π; angles around a point sum to 2π. If the minor central angle is θ, its reflex partner is 2π−θ. The angle at the centre is not generally the angle at the circumference.

Use radians in trigonometric calculations

Set the calculator to RAD before evaluating sine, cosine or an inverse trigonometric ratio for a radian question. Keep unrounded intermediate values. An inverse ratio needs the branch allowed by the geometry.
lessons.method:
1. Mark the angle and decide whether it is minor, reflex or part of a triangle.
  2. Convert all angle measures to a consistent unit.
  3. Use θ=s/r or an angle sum; retain exact fractions of π.
  4. Check the size against the diagram without treating the sketch as a scale drawing.

The written questions combine these angle skills with the later arc, area and boundary methods in this chapter.
mistakes: Do not put a degree value directly into a radian formula.
Use π, not 2π, as the angle sum of a triangle.
Check whether the required angle is the reflex partner.
Calculator mode matters even when the final answer is in centimetres.

examples.title: Use the definition before a formula
examples.question: An arc of length 10.5 m lies on a circle of radius 7 m. Find its central angle.
examples.solution:
\[\theta=\frac{10.5}{7}=\frac32\text{ radians}.\]

The ratio uses two lengths in the same unit. It is not 1.5 degrees.

examples.title: Exact conversion in both directions
examples.question: Convert 150° to radians and \(7\pi/4\) radians to degrees.
examples.solution:
\[150\frac{\pi}{180}=\frac{5\pi}{6},\qquad \frac{7\pi}{4}\frac{180}{\pi}=315^\circ.\]

Work with the exact fraction before using decimals.

examples.title: Keep minor and reflex angles separate
examples.question: A minor central angle is \(2\pi/5\). Find the reflex angle between the same radii.
examples.solution:
\[2\pi-\frac{2\pi}{5}=\frac{8\pi}{5}.\]

The result is greater than π and less than 2π, as a reflex angle should be.

examples.title: An inverse ratio with the correct mode
examples.question: An acute angle in a right-angled triangle has opposite side 4 cm and adjacent side 3 cm. Find the angle in radians to 3 significant figures.
examples.solution:
\[\theta=\tan^{-1}\!\left(\frac43\right)=0.927295\ldots\text{ radians}.\]

Thus θ=0.927 radians to 3 significant figures. The acute condition selects the angle between 0 and π/2.

lessons.title: Arc length, sector perimeter and rolling distance
lessons.summary: Choose the correct arc and include only the actual straight edges of the boundary.
lessons.objective: Use s = rθ for minor or major arcs, reconstruct missing data and distinguish arc length from sector perimeter.
lessons.before: Recall radian conversion and the distinction between a radius, diameter, chord and arc.
lessons.ideas:
An arc scales with its radius and angle

\[s=r\theta\qquad(\theta\text{ in radians}).\]

For the same radius, a major arc uses the reflex angle, not the smaller angle drawn between the radii.

A sector includes two radial edges

For a sector with \(0<\theta<2\pi\),

\[P=2r+r\theta.\]

The arc alone is not the sector perimeter. A segment has a chord instead of those two radii; its boundary is treated in the segments lesson.

Reverse the calculation

Use r=s/θ or θ=s/r, retaining consistent units. When the perimeter and arc length are given, the two straight radii together have length P−s.

Several rotations describe travel

N full turns give a total angle of 2πN and an arc-travel distance of 2πrN. For a wheel rolling without slipping this equals the ground distance. Cumulative travel can involve more than one turn; it is not the area of a sector covering the same region repeatedly.
lessons.method:
1. Identify the centre and radius of the required arc.
  2. Find its angle in radians, using the reflex angle if needed.
  3. Calculate the arc with s=rθ.
  4. For a perimeter, trace the complete boundary and add each exposed straight edge once.
mistakes: An arc is not the straight chord between its endpoints.
A sector perimeter normally needs two radii.
Use the major angle for a major arc.
For rolling distance, use the radius rather than the diameter in rθ.

examples.title: An arc and a complete sector boundary
examples.question: A sector has radius 6 cm and angle 0.8 radians. Find its arc length and perimeter.
examples.solution:
\[s=6(0.8)=4.8\text{ cm},\qquad P=12+4.8=16.8\text{ cm}.\]

The two radial edges account for the difference.

examples.title: Recover a radius exactly
examples.question: An arc has length \(5\pi\) cm and central angle \(5\pi/6\). Find the radius and sector perimeter.
examples.solution:
\[r=\frac{5\pi}{5\pi/6}=6,\qquad P=12+5\pi\text{ cm}.\]

The angle is already in radians, and π cancels in the radius calculation.

examples.title: Use the reflex angle for the major arc
examples.question: A circle has radius 4 cm and minor central angle \(\pi/3\). Find the major arc length and major-sector perimeter.
examples.solution:
\[\theta_{\rm major}=2\pi-\frac\pi3=\frac{5\pi}3,\qquad s=\frac{20\pi}3.\]

The major-sector perimeter is \(8+20\pi/3\) cm. Its two radial edges remain part of the boundary.

examples.title: Count all the turns
examples.question: A wheel of radius 0.35 m rolls without slipping through 12.5 turns. Find the exact distance travelled.
examples.solution:
\[\theta=12.5(2\pi)=25\pi,\qquad d=\frac7{20}(25\pi)=\frac{35\pi}{4}\text{ m}.\]

The angle measures accumulated rotation, so it can exceed 2π.

lessons.title: Sector area and reconstruction
lessons.summary: Use the sector fraction of a circle, combine area and arc data, and check geometric restrictions.
lessons.objective: Find sector areas, reconstruct radius and angle and model a fixed sector perimeter using a quadratic.
lessons.before: Recall the area of a circle, radian measure, algebraic rearrangement and completing the square.
lessons.ideas:
A sector is a fraction of a circle

Its angle is θ out of a complete 2π turn, so

\[A=\frac{\theta}{2\pi}\,\pi r^2=\frac12r^2\theta.\]

This formula uses radians. Combining it with s=rθ gives \(A=\tfrac12rs\), which can simplify reconstruction.

Reverse two measurements

From A and θ, find r²=2A/θ and take the positive radius. From area and arc length, use r=2A/s, then θ=s/r. From area and perimeter, solve both conditions and reject roots violating r>0 or the stated angle range.

A fixed perimeter gives a quadratic

For a sector of perimeter P, with 0<θ<2π,

\[\theta=\frac{P-2r}{r},\qquad A=\frac P2r-r^2.\]

Completing the square finds an area bound without calculus. Check that the radius attaining it gives an angle in the allowed range.
lessons.method:
1. Record which angle belongs to the sector, in radians.
  2. Use A=½r²θ or A=½rs to match the available data.
  3. If reconstructing, solve for the positive radius and then the angle.
  4. Check both original measurements and any minor/reflex restriction.
mistakes: Sector area uses r²; arc length uses r.
Do not omit the factor ½.
A negative algebraic radius is not a geometric solution.
Area and perimeter have different units.

examples.title: Area with a non-special radian angle
examples.question: Find the area of a sector with radius 5 cm and angle 1.2 radians.
examples.solution:
\[A=\frac12(5^2)(1.2)=15\text{ cm}^2.\]

No conversion is needed: 1.2 is already a radian measure.

examples.title: A radius from an exact area
examples.question: A sector has area \(18\pi\) cm² and angle \(\pi/4\). Find its radius and perimeter.
examples.solution:
\[r^2=\frac{2(18\pi)}{\pi/4}=144,\qquad r=12.\]

The arc length is 3π cm, so the perimeter is \(24+3\pi\) cm.

examples.title: Area and arc length work together
examples.question: A sector has area 40 cm² and arc length 10 cm. Find its radius, angle and perimeter.
examples.solution:
\[r=\frac{2A}{s}=8,\qquad\theta=\frac{10}8=\frac54.\]

The perimeter is 2(8)+10=26 cm. Substituting into ½r²θ gives the original area.

examples.title: An area maximum without differentiating
examples.question: A sector has perimeter 20 cm and angle between 0 and 2π. Find its greatest possible area.
examples.solution:
\[\theta=\frac{20-2r}{r},\qquad A=10r-r^2=25-(r-5)^2.\]

Thus A≤25 cm². Equality occurs at r=5, giving θ=2 radians, which satisfies the stated restriction. The maximum is therefore attained.

lessons.title: Chords, triangles and circular segments
lessons.summary: Separate a sector from its triangle and decide whether the requested region is minor or major.
lessons.objective: Find chord lengths and minor or major segment areas and perimeters using the correct radian angle.
lessons.before: Recall sine, cosine, isosceles triangles, sector formulas and exact special-angle values.
lessons.ideas:
A chord comes from two right triangles

Bisect the isosceles central triangle. For a minor central angle θ,

\[c=2r\sin\frac\theta2,\qquad d=r\cos\frac\theta2,\]

where c is the chord length and d the perpendicular distance from the centre to the chord.

A minor segment is sector minus triangle

For 0<θ<π,

\[A_{\rm triangle}=\frac12r^2\sin\theta,\qquad A_{\rm minor}=\frac12r^2(\theta-\sin\theta).\]

Use radians both in θ and in the trigonometric calculation. At θ=π the segment is a semicircle.

Its perimeter is arc plus chord

\[P_{\rm minor}=r\theta+c.\]

The two radii inside the construction are not on the segment boundary.

A major segment is the complementary region

\[A_{\rm major}=\pi r^2-A_{\rm minor},\qquad P_{\rm major}=r(2\pi-\theta)+c.\]

Using the complement avoids subtracting an unsigned triangle from a reflex sector incorrectly.
lessons.method:
1. Mark the chord and the relevant central angle.
  2. Find the central triangle area or chord length using radians.
  3. For a minor segment, subtract the triangle from its sector.
  4. For a major segment, use the circle complement and the major arc; include the chord once.
mistakes: A segment is bounded by an arc and a chord, not two radii.
The half-angle belongs in the chord formula.
Use the complementary area for a major segment.
Keep full calculator precision until the final rounding.

examples.title: See the triangle being removed
examples.question: Find the minor segment area for radius 4 cm and angle π/2.
examples.solution:
\[A_{\rm sector}=4\pi,\qquad A_{\rm triangle}=8,\qquad A_{\rm segment}=4\pi-8\text{ cm}^2.\]

The unshaded central triangle is not part of the segment.

examples.title: A chord equal to the radius
examples.question: A circle has radius 6 cm and chord length 6 cm. Find the minor angle and the minor segment area and perimeter.
examples.solution:
The central triangle is equilateral, so θ=π/3.

\[A=6\pi-9\sqrt3\text{ cm}^2,\qquad P=6+2\pi\text{ cm}.\]

The perimeter uses the chord 6 and arc 2π, without adding either radius.

examples.title: Choose the major region
examples.question: A circle has radius 3 cm and chord length \(3\sqrt3\) cm. Find the major segment area and perimeter.
examples.solution:
Since \(\sin(\theta/2)=\sqrt3/2\), the minor angle is 2π/3. Hence

\[A_{\rm minor}=3\pi-\frac{9\sqrt3}{4},\]\[A_{\rm major}=6\pi+\frac{9\sqrt3}{4},\qquad P_{\rm major}=4\pi+3\sqrt3.\]

The two segment areas sum to 9π.

examples.title: Round the area, not the intermediate sine
examples.question: Find the minor segment area for radius 8 cm and angle 0.9 radians, to 3 significant figures.
examples.solution:
\[A=32\left(0.9-\sin0.9\right)=3.733538\ldots\text{ cm}^2.\]

Therefore A=3.73 cm². Using degree mode or rounding sin(0.9) too early gives a different result.

lessons.title: Composite boundaries, overlaps and modelling
lessons.summary: Combine sector and triangle pieces, trace the exposed boundary and check the geometry of a model.
lessons.objective: Find composite areas and perimeters, handle annular sectors and overlaps and form consistent geometric models.
lessons.before: Recall sector, triangle and segment formulas, tangency and the distinction between a union and an overlap.
lessons.ideas:
Trace the boundary before adding lengths

Identify every arc's own centre, radius and angle. Add only exposed boundary pieces; shared joins and construction lines are internal. A circular cut-out removes area but adds an inner boundary to the perimeter when that boundary is included in the question.

An annular sector

For outer radius R, inner radius r and angle θ with 0<θ<2π,

\[A=\frac12(R^2-r^2)\theta,\qquad P=(R+r)\theta+2(R-r).\]

There are two arcs and two radial gaps; the gaps are not full radii.

Overlap and union are different areas

Two intersecting circles can be split along their common chord. Calculate each contributing segment with its own radius and central angle. The overlap is counted once; for a union use

\[A_{\rm union}=A_1+A_2-A_{\rm overlap}.\]

Check a model against the diagram

Use tangency to obtain right angles, positive lengths and permitted angle ranges. Similar figures scale lengths by k and areas by k². A taut rope around a convex bundle has exposed straight tangent pieces and curved contact pieces; interior joins do not count.
lessons.method:
1. Label radii, angles and the actual boundary.
  2. Break the area into non-overlapping pieces, or subtract an explicitly identified overlap.
  3. Sum each exposed straight or curved length once.
  4. Check units, positivity, angle restrictions and all original measurements after solving.
mistakes: Do not count an internal diameter in the outside perimeter.
Subtract an overlap once when finding a union.
Different arcs may have different centres and radii.
A length scale factor is not the corresponding area scale factor.

examples.title: Two radii, two arcs and two gaps
examples.question: An annular sector has outer radius 6 cm, inner radius 2 cm and angle 0.7 radians. Find its area and perimeter.
examples.solution:
\[A=\frac12(36-4)(0.7)=11.2\text{ cm}^2,\]\[P=(6+2)(0.7)+2(6-2)=13.6\text{ cm}.\]

The two straight gaps each have length 4.

examples.title: A shared edge is not an outside edge
examples.question: A semicircle of radius 3 cm is attached along the 6 cm top edge of a 6 cm by 4 cm rectangle. Find the total area and outside perimeter.
examples.solution:
\[A=24+\frac{9\pi}{2}\text{ cm}^2,\qquad P=6+4+4+3\pi=14+3\pi\text{ cm}.\]

The shared diameter is inside the figure and is excluded from the outside perimeter.

examples.title: An overlap consists of two segments
examples.question: Two circles have radius 4 cm and centres 4 cm apart. Find their overlap area, union area and the external perimeter of the union.
examples.solution:
Joining either intersection to both centres gives an equilateral triangle. Each minor central angle is 2π/3. Thus

\[A_{\rm overlap}=2\left(\frac{16\pi}{3}-4\sqrt3\right)=\frac{32\pi}{3}-8\sqrt3,\]\[A_{\rm union}=\frac{64\pi}{3}+8\sqrt3.\]

The exposed boundary consists of two major arcs, each of angle 4π/3, so \(P_{\rm union}=32\pi/3\) cm.

examples.title: A rope counts exposed contact arcs
examples.question: Three equal pipes of radius 3 cm touch pairwise. A taut rope of negligible thickness surrounds them. Find its length, then the radius of seven equal pipes held by the same rope in a one-plus-six bundle.
examples.solution:
For three pipes the straight portions total 6r, and the contact arcs together subtend a complete turn. Therefore

\[L=6r+2\pi r=18+6\pi.\]

For seven pipes, the outer-centre hexagon has perimeter 12ρ and the exposed contact arcs still total 2πρ. Reusing the rope gives

\[\rho=\frac{18+6\pi}{12+2\pi}=\frac{3(3+\pi)}{6+\pi}\text{ cm}.\]

The centre pipe contributes no exposed boundary.

questions.title: Exact conversion in both directions
questions.prompt_html: Convert 150° to radians and \(\frac{7 \pi}{4}\) radians to degrees. Give exact answers.
questions.answer_html:
First angle in radians: \(\frac{5 \pi}{6}\)

Second angle in degrees: \(315\)
questions.solution_html: Multiply degrees by π/180 and radians by 180/π. Keep the exact multiples of π until cancelling.
questions.hint_html: Use π radians = 180 degrees; distinguish a triangle angle sum from a complete turn.

questions.title: Arc ratio and reflex partner
questions.prompt_html: A minor arc has length 12 cm on a circle of radius 8 cm. Find its central angle and the reflex angle between the same radii.
questions.answer_html:
Minor angle in radians: \(\frac{3}{2}\)

Reflex angle in radians: \(- \frac{3}{2} + 2 \pi\)
questions.solution_html: The definition gives θ=s/r=\(\frac{3}{2}\). Subtract it from a complete 2π turn for the reflex partner.
questions.hint_html: Use π radians = 180 degrees; distinguish a triangle angle sum from a complete turn.

Complete correct answer for Reflex angle in radians.

questions.title: Complete a triangle angle sum
questions.prompt_html: Two angles of a triangle are \(\frac{\pi}{6}\) and \(\frac{\pi}{4}\) radians. Find its third angle, in radians and in degrees.
questions.answer_html:
Third angle in radians: \(\frac{7 \pi}{12}\)

Third angle in degrees: \(105\)
questions.solution_html: Subtract the two angles from π, then convert the remainder to degrees. Do not use a 2π triangle angle sum.
questions.hint_html: Use π radians = 180 degrees; distinguish a triangle angle sum from a complete turn.

marking_criteria.description_html: Complete correct answer for Third angle in radians.

questions.title: Recognise one radian
questions.prompt_html: A circle has radius 5 cm. An arc of length 5 cm subtends which angle? What angle is subtended by an arc 3 times as long on this circle?
questions.answer_html:
Angle of the first arc: 1 radian

Angle of the longer arc in radians: \(3\)
questions.solution_html: An arc equal to the radius defines one radian. At fixed radius, multiplying the arc length multiplies its angle by the same factor.
questions.hint_html: Use π radians = 180 degrees; distinguish a triangle angle sum from a complete turn.

questions.title: Arc length and complete sector perimeter
questions.prompt_html: A sector has radius 7 cm and angle \(\frac{4}{5}\) radians. Find its arc length and perimeter exactly.
questions.answer_html:
Arc length (cm): \(\frac{28}{5}\)

Sector perimeter (cm): \(\frac{98}{5}\)
questions.solution_html: Use s=rθ for the curved edge and add both radii for the complete sector perimeter.
questions.hint_html: Use the angle of the required arc in s=rθ, then add only the stated straight boundary.

questions.title: Reverse an exact arc calculation
questions.prompt_html: A sector arc is \(7 \pi\) cm long and its angle is \(\frac{7 \pi}{4}\) radians. Find the radius and sector perimeter.
questions.answer_html:
Radius (cm): \(4\)

Sector perimeter (cm): \(8 + 7 \pi\)
questions.solution_html: Divide the arc length by its radian angle, then add twice that radius to the arc length.
questions.hint_html: Use the angle of the required arc in s=rθ, then add only the stated straight boundary.

marking_criteria.description_html: Complete correct answer for Sector perimeter (cm).

questions.title: Both arcs between the same endpoints
questions.prompt_html: A circle has radius 3 cm and minor central angle \(\frac{\pi}{3}\). Find the minor and major arc lengths.
questions.answer_html:
Minor arc length (cm): \(\pi\)

Major arc length (cm): \(5 \pi\)
questions.solution_html: The minor and major angles sum to 2π. The two arc lengths should add to the full circumference.
questions.hint_html: Use the angle of the required arc in s=rθ, then add only the stated straight boundary.

questions.title: Rolling without slipping
questions.prompt_html: A wheel of radius \(\frac{2}{5}\) m rolls without slipping through \(\frac{15}{4}\) turns. Find its accumulated angle in radians and its distance travelled.
questions.answer_html:
Accumulated angle in radians: \(\frac{15 \pi}{2}\)

Distance travelled (m): \(3 \pi\)
questions.solution_html: Multiply the number of turns by 2π, then multiply that accumulated radian angle by the radius.
questions.hint_html: Use the angle of the required arc in s=rθ, then add only the stated straight boundary.

marking_criteria.description_html: Complete correct answer for Accumulated angle in radians.

questions.title: Sector area and arc length
questions.prompt_html: A sector has radius 6 cm and angle \(\frac{\pi}{3}\). Find its area and arc length exactly.
questions.answer_html:
Sector area (cm²): \(6 \pi\)

Arc length (cm): \(2 \pi\)
questions.solution_html: The area is ½r²θ, whereas the arc length is rθ. Keep the squared and unsquared lengths distinct.
questions.hint_html: Use A=½r²θ or A=½rs; retain the geometric restrictions when reconstructing.

questions.title: An exact radius from area and angle
questions.prompt_html: A sector has area \(16 \pi\) cm² and angle \(\frac{\pi}{2}\). Find its radius and perimeter exactly.
questions.answer_html:
Radius (cm): \(8\)

Sector perimeter (cm): \(4 \pi + 16\)
questions.solution_html: Find r²=2A/θ and choose the positive radius. Then use 2r+rθ for the perimeter.
questions.hint_html: Use A=½r²θ or A=½rs; retain the geometric restrictions when reconstructing.

questions.title: Reconstruct from two measurements
questions.prompt_html: A sector has arc length 12 cm and area 30 cm². Find its radius, angle and perimeter.
questions.answer_html:
Radius (cm): \(5\)

Angle in radians: \(\frac{12}{5}\)

Sector perimeter (cm): \(22\)
questions.solution_html: Combine A=½rs with s=rθ. Recover the radius first, then the angle and the complete boundary.
questions.hint_html: Use A=½r²θ or A=½rs; retain the geometric restrictions when reconstructing.

questions.title: A fixed-perimeter area model
questions.prompt_html: A sector has perimeter 24 cm and 0<θ<2π. Give its area as a polynomial in radius r, then find the radius, angle and area at its maximum.
questions.answer_html:
Area expression in r: \(- r^{2} + 12 r\)

Radius at the maximum (cm): \(6\)

Angle at the maximum in radians: \(2\)

Maximum area (cm²): \(36\)
questions.solution_html:
\[A=12r-r^2=36-(r-6)^2.\]

The maximum is attained at the stated radius; its angle is 2 radians, within the allowed range.
questions.hint_html: Use A=½r²θ or A=½rs; retain the geometric restrictions when reconstructing.

questions.prompt_html: A circle has radius 4 cm and minor central angle \(\frac{\pi}{3}\). Find the exact area and perimeter of the minor segment.
questions.answer_html:
Minor segment area (cm²): \(- 4 \sqrt{3} + \frac{8 \pi}{3}\)

Minor segment perimeter (cm): \(4 + \frac{4 \pi}{3}\)
questions.solution_html: Subtract the central triangle from the sector for area. For perimeter add the chord, not the two radii, to the minor arc.

questions.prompt_html:
Sector OAB has centre O. The arc AB has length \(\frac{36}{5}\) cm and the sector perimeter is \(\frac{96}{5}\) cm. AB is the minor arc.

  1. Find the radius and the central angle in radians.

    [3]

  2. Find the area and perimeter of the minor segment, each to 3 significant figures.

    [4]
questions.answer_html:
(a) \(6\) cm; \(\frac{6}{5}\) radians
(b) \(\frac{108}{5} - 18 \sin{\left(\frac{6}{5} \right)}\) cm² (approximately \(4.82\) cm²). \(12 \sin{\left(\frac{3}{5} \right)} + \frac{36}{5}\) cm (approximately \(14.0\) cm).

(a)

First recover the radius from the two straight radii in the perimeter.

\[r=6\]\[\theta=\frac sr=\frac{6}{5}\]

\[A=\frac12r^2(\theta-\sin\theta)=\frac{108}{5} - 18 \sin{\left(\frac{6}{5} \right)}\]

The chord is \(12 \sin{\left(\frac{3}{5} \right)}\), so the perimeter is \(12 \sin{\left(\frac{3}{5} \right)} + \frac{36}{5}\).

questions.title: Recovering a hidden radius
questions.prompt_html:
Sector OAB has centre O. The arc AB has length \(\frac{49}{5}\) cm and the sector perimeter is \(\frac{119}{5}\) cm. AB is the minor arc.

  1. Find the radius and the central angle in radians.

    [3]

  2. Find the area and perimeter of the minor segment, each to 3 significant figures.

    [4]
questions.answer_html:
(a) \(7\) cm; \(\frac{7}{5}\) radians
(b) \(\frac{343}{10} - \frac{49 \sin{\left(\frac{7}{5} \right)}}{2}\) cm² (approximately \(10.2\) cm²). \(14 \sin{\left(\frac{7}{10} \right)} + \frac{49}{5}\) cm (approximately \(18.8\) cm).
questions.solution_html:
(a)

First recover the radius from the two straight radii in the perimeter.

\[r=7\]\[\theta=\frac sr=\frac{7}{5}\]

(b)

Subtract the isosceles triangle from the sector. The angle must be in radians.

\[A=\frac12r^2(\theta-\sin\theta)=\frac{343}{10} - \frac{49 \sin{\left(\frac{7}{5} \right)}}{2}\]

The chord is \(14 \sin{\left(\frac{7}{10} \right)}\), so the perimeter is \(14 \sin{\left(\frac{7}{10} \right)} + \frac{49}{5}\).
questions.hint_html: Use the data to find r before using trigonometry.

questions.title: Which sector is reflex?
questions.prompt_html:
A major sector OAB has perimeter \(10 + \frac{15 \pi}{2}\) cm and area \(\frac{75 \pi}{4}\) cm². Its radius is r cm and its angle is θ radians, with \(\pi<\theta<2\pi\).

  1. Find r and the reflex angle θ exactly. Justify your choice if your equation has two roots.

    [4]

  2. Find the exact area of triangle AOB.

    [2]
questions.answer_html:
(a) \(5\) cm; \(\frac{3 \pi}{2}\) radians
(b) \(\frac{25}{2}\) cm²
questions.solution_html:
(a)

Eliminate θ between \(P=r(2+\theta)\) and \(A=\frac12r^2\theta\).

\[2r^2-\left(10 + \frac{15 \pi}{2}\right)r+\frac{75 \pi}{2}=0\]

The candidate radii are \(5\) and \(\frac{15 \pi}{4}\). The latter gives \(\frac{8}{3 \pi}\) radians, which is not reflex. Retain the radius giving \(\pi<\theta<2\pi\).

(b)

Use the smaller angle \(\frac{\pi}{2}\) in the triangle.

\[A_{\triangle}=\frac12r^2\sin(2\pi-\theta)=\frac{25}{2}\]
questions.hint_html: Both positive roots must be checked against the stated angle range.

marking_criteria.description_html: Solves the quadratic, retaining both candidates initially.
Uses a positive triangle area with the smaller angle.

questions.title: A chord determines the larger region
questions.prompt_html:
A circle has centre O, radius \(5\) cm and chord AB of length \(5 \sqrt{3}\) cm.

  1. Find the minor angle AOB exactly.

    [2]

  2. Find the exact area of the major segment bounded by AB and the major arc.

    [3]
questions.answer_html:
(a) \(\frac{2 \pi}{3}\) radians
(b) \(\frac{25 \sqrt{3}}{4} + \frac{50 \pi}{3}\) cm²
questions.solution_html:
(a)

Bisect the isosceles triangle: \(\sin(\frac{\theta}{2})=\frac{AB}{2r}\).

\[\theta=\frac{2 \pi}{3}\]

(b)

Subtract the minor segment from the full circle; do not subtract only a sector.

\[A_{\rm major}=\pi r^2-\frac12r^2(\theta-\sin\theta)=\frac{25 \sqrt{3}}{4} + \frac{50 \pi}{3}\]
questions.hint_html: Find the minor segment first, then use the whole circle.

questions.prompt_html:
OBC is a sector of radius \(5\) cm. H is on OC and BH is perpendicular to OC. angle BOC is \(\frac{\pi}{6}\) radians.

  1. Find angle BOC in radians and the length OH.

    [3]

  2. Find the area and perimeter bounded by HC, minor arc CB and BH. Give exact expressions.

    [4]
questions.answer_html:
(a) \(\frac{\pi}{6}\) radians; \(\frac{5 \sqrt{3}}{2}\) cm
(b) \(- \frac{25 \sqrt{3}}{8} + \frac{25 \pi}{12}\) cm² (approximately \(1.13\) cm²). \(- \frac{5 \sqrt{3}}{2} + \frac{5 \pi}{6} + \frac{15}{2}\) cm (approximately \(5.79\) cm).
questions.solution_html:
(a)

The radial angle equals the given angle.

\[\theta=\frac{\pi}{6}\]\[OH=r\cos\theta=\frac{5 \sqrt{3}}{2}\]

(b)

Subtract right triangle OHB from the sector. The straight boundary consists of HC and BH.

\[A=- \frac{25 \sqrt{3}}{8} + \frac{25 \pi}{12}\]\[P=- \frac{5 \sqrt{3}}{2} + \frac{5 \pi}{6} + \frac{15}{2}\]
questions.hint_html: The removed right triangle has legs r cos θ and r sin θ.

questions.prompt_html:
A minor sector OAB has acute angle θ. Its triangle OAB has area \(4\) cm² and its sector has area \(8\theta\) cm².

Angles are measured in radians.

\[A=\frac12r^2(\theta-\sin\theta)=-4 + \frac{4 \pi}{3}\]

(b)

questions.title: A straight cut dividing a sector equally
questions.prompt_html:
OAB is a sector of radius \(8\) cm with angle \(\frac{\pi}{6}\) radians. D and E lie on OA and OB, with \(OD=OE=kr,\quad 0<k<1\). Triangle ODE and the rest of the sector have equal areas.

  1. Find k to 4 significant figures.

    [3]

  2. Now allow θ to vary with \(0<\theta<\frac{\pi}{2}\). Prove that \(\frac{1}{\sqrt2}<k<\frac{\sqrt\pi}{2}\). You may use that \(\frac{\theta}{\sin\theta}\) is strictly increasing, with limiting values 1 and \(\frac{\pi}{2}\) at the two ends of this interval.

    [3]

  3. For the original angle, find the perimeter of the outer region as an exact expression.

    [3]
questions.answer_html:
(a) \(0.7236\)
(b) \(\frac{1}{\sqrt2}<k<\frac{\sqrt\pi}{2}\)
(c) \(- \frac{8 \sqrt{6} \sqrt{\pi}}{3} + \frac{8 \sqrt{6} \sqrt{\pi} \left(- \frac{\sqrt{2}}{4} + \frac{\sqrt{6}}{4}\right)}{3} + \frac{4 \pi}{3} + 16\) cm
questions.solution_html:
(a)

Triangle ODE has area \(\frac12 k^2r^2\sin\theta\). It is half the whole sector area, so

\[k^2=\frac{\theta}{2\sin\theta}=\frac{\pi}{6}\]

Take the positive square root, since k is a ratio of lengths.

(b)

The ratio \(\frac{\theta}{\sin\theta}\) increases from its limiting value 1 to \(\frac{\pi}{2}\). Hence \(\frac12<k^2<\frac{\pi}{4}\). All quantities are positive, so taking square roots preserves the inequalities. The endpoints are not attained.

(c)

The outer boundary contains the full arc AB, the two remaining radial pieces and the interior chord DE. Add all four contributions.

In isosceles triangle OPA, OP = AP = x. Applying the cosine rule at O gives \(x^2=x^2+R^2-2xR\cos\theta\). Since R is positive, \(R=2x\cos\theta\). Multiply by θ to find the arc.

The area is sector OAB minus triangle OPA. For the perimeter, PA = OP = x, so \(PA+PB=x+(R-x)=R\).

questions.title: Projection creates the inner radius
questions.prompt_html:
OAB is a sector with radius \(6\) cm and angle \(\frac{3}{5}\) radians. C lies on OB, with AC perpendicular to OB. Arc CD has centre O, with D on OA. The shaded region is bounded by CA, AD and arc DC.

  1. Find OC and AD in terms of the given radius and angle.

    [2]

  2. Find the area and perimeter bounded by CA, AD and arc DC, to 3 significant figures.

    [5]
questions.answer_html:
(a) \(6 \cos{\left(\frac{3}{5} \right)}\) cm; \(6 - 6 \cos{\left(\frac{3}{5} \right)}\) cm
(b) \(- \frac{54 \cos^{2}{\left(\frac{3}{5} \right)}}{5} + 18 \sin{\left(\frac{3}{5} \right)} \cos{\left(\frac{3}{5} \right)}\) cm² (approximately \(1.03\) cm²). \(- \frac{12 \cos{\left(\frac{3}{5} \right)}}{5} + 6 \sin{\left(\frac{3}{5} \right)} + 6\) cm (approximately \(7.41\) cm).
questions.solution_html:
(a)

OC is the projection of OA onto OB. Since OC = OD, subtract OD from OA to obtain AD.

\[OC=6 \cos{\left(\frac{3}{5} \right)}\]\[AD=6 - 6 \cos{\left(\frac{3}{5} \right)}\]

(b)

The outer shape OCA is a right triangle; the removed shape OCD is a sector of radius OC, not OA.

\[A=- \frac{27}{5} - \frac{27 \cos{\left(\frac{6}{5} \right)}}{5} + 9 \sin{\left(\frac{6}{5} \right)}\]

For the perimeter use CA = r sin θ, AD = r − r cos θ and arc DC = rθ cos θ.

\[P=- \frac{12 \cos{\left(\frac{3}{5} \right)}}{5} + 6 \sin{\left(\frac{3}{5} \right)} + 6\]

questions.title: Three adjacent sectors and two exposed steps
questions.prompt_html:
Three sectors share O and occupy consecutive angles θ, 2θ and θ. Their radii are r, 2r and r respectively. Their union is one plate, with \(0<\theta<\frac{\pi}{4}\). Its perimeter is \(49\) cm and its area is \(\frac{245}{2}\) cm².

Angles are measured in radians.

  1. Show that the plate has area 5r²θ and perimeter r(4 + 6θ).

    [4]

  2. Use the given measurements to find r and θ, explaining why any other algebraic solution is invalid.

    [4]
questions.answer_html:
(a) \(A=5r^2\theta,\quad P=r(4+6\theta)\)
(b) \(7\) cm; \(\frac{1}{2}\) radians
questions.solution_html:
(a)

The three sector areas are \(\frac12r^2\theta,\ 4r^2\theta,\ \frac12r^2\theta\). The arcs total 6rθ. Two outer radii and two steps each have length r.

(b)

Eliminate θ to give \(20r^2-5Pr+6A=0\). The candidate radii are \(7\) and \(\frac{21}{4}\). The alternative implies \(\frac{8}{9}\) radians, which exceeds \(\frac{\pi}{4}\).
questions.hint_html: The two changes of radius each contribute a boundary length r.

questions.title: A horizontal bridge between two circular arcs
questions.prompt_html:
A plate has boundary arc AB, line BC, arc CD and line DA. Both arcs have centre O. A and D lie on the negative horizontal ray from O; C lies vertically above O. \(OA=OB=10\text{ cm},\quad OC=OD=5\text{ cm}\). BC is horizontal. B is above and to the left of O.

  1. Find the exact angle AOB in radians.

    [2]

  2. Find the exact perimeter and area of the plate.

    [6]
questions.answer_html:
(a) \(\frac{\pi}{6}\) radians
(b) \(5 + 5 \sqrt{3} + \frac{25 \pi}{6}\) cm; \(\frac{25 \pi}{12} + \frac{25 \sqrt{3}}{2}\) cm²
questions.solution_html:
(a)

BC is horizontal at height ρ, so \(R\sin\theta=\rho\). Since the angle is acute, \(\frac{\pi}{6}\) is the required value.

(b)

The perimeter uses outer arc AB, horizontal BC, inner quarter-arc CD and AD. For area, take the sector OAB plus triangle OBC and subtract the inner quarter-disc.

\[P=5 + 5 \sqrt{3} + \frac{25 \pi}{6}\]\[A=\frac12R^2\theta+\frac12R\rho\cos\theta-\frac14\pi\rho^2=\frac{25 \pi}{12} + \frac{25 \sqrt{3}}{2}\]
questions.hint_html: The angle COD is π/2; the angle AOB must be found from the height.

questions.title: Two facing sectors form a bridge plate
questions.prompt_html:
A, B, C and D lie in that order on a horizontal line. \(AB=CD=r=\frac{2}{3}\text{ cm},\quad BC=3\text{ cm}\). Arc BF has centre A and arc CE has centre D; each subtends \(\frac{\pi}{3}\) radians above the line. E and F are joined. The plate boundary is BC, arc CE, EF and arc FB.

  1. Find EF exactly and the plate area to 3 significant figures.

    [5]

  2. Instead, the same gap BC is used and the perimeter is \(\frac{7 \pi}{9} + \frac{43}{6}\) cm. Find the new radius exactly.

    [3]
questions.answer_html:
(a) \(\frac{11}{3}\) cm; \(- \frac{4 \pi}{27} + \frac{4 \sqrt{3}}{3}\) cm² (approximately \(1.84\) cm²).
(b) \(\frac{7}{6}\) cm
questions.solution_html:
(a)

Both upper endpoints have height r sin θ. Their separation is \(EF=2r+g-2r\cos\theta\). Take the trapezium BCEF and subtract the two minor circular segments between its sloping sides and arcs.

\[A=r\sin\theta(2r+g-r\cos\theta)-r^2\theta=- \frac{4 \pi}{27} + \frac{4 \sqrt{3}}{3}\]

(b)

The perimeter is \(2g+2r(1-\cos\theta+\theta)\). The gap is unchanged; solve the resulting linear equation for the new radius.
questions.hint_html: The arcs curve into the trapezium, so their segments must be removed.

Uses the trapezium minus two segments.
Forms the boundary formula, including both arcs.

questions.title: Two arcs with unequal centres on the baseline
questions.prompt_html:
X and Y lie on the horizontal line AB, with Y to the right of X. \(XC=4\text{ cm},\quad YC=YA=6\text{ cm}\), and XC is perpendicular to AB. A is to the left of X, and B is to the right, with XB = XC. Arc BC is centred at X; arc CA is centred at Y. The region lies above AB.

  1. Find XY exactly and angle XYC in radians.

    [3]

  2. Find the perimeter and area of ABC, to 3 significant figures.

    [6]
questions.answer_html:
(a) \(2 \sqrt{5}\) cm; \(\sin^{-1}{\left(\frac{2}{3} \right)}\) radians
(b) \(- 2 \sqrt{5} + 6 \sin^{-1}{\left(\frac{2}{3} \right)} + 2 \pi + 10\) cm (approximately \(16.2\) cm). \(- 4 \sqrt{5} + 4 \pi + 18 \sin^{-1}{\left(\frac{2}{3} \right)}\) cm² (approximately \(16.8\) cm²).
questions.solution_html:
(a)

XC is perpendicular to XY. Use Pythagoras and the ratio XC/YC.

\[XY=2 \sqrt{5}\]\[\angle XYC=\sin^{-1}{\left(\frac{2}{3} \right)}\]

(b)

AB = a + b − XY. Add a quarter-circle arc of radius a and an arc of radius b subtending angle XYC. The area is the quarter-disc at X plus the sector at Y, minus triangle XYC.

\[P=- 2 \sqrt{5} + 6 \sin^{-1}{\left(\frac{2}{3} \right)} + 2 \pi + 10\]\[A=- 4 \sqrt{5} + 4 \pi + 18 \sin^{-1}{\left(\frac{2}{3} \right)}\]
questions.hint_html: The two arcs do not share a radius or central angle.

Uses different radii and angles for the two arcs.

questions.title: A straight base and two circular sides
questions.prompt_html:
A and B are \(6\) cm apart. The upper intersection of the circles of radius AB centred at A and B is C. The boundary is straight AB, minor arc BC centred at A and minor arc CA centred at B.

  1. Find the exact perimeter of the region.

    [3]

  2. Find the exact area of the region.

    [3]
questions.answer_html:
(a) \(6 + 4 \pi\) cm
(b) \(- 9 \sqrt{3} + 12 \pi\) cm²
questions.solution_html:
(a)

The triangle ABC is equilateral because both arcs have radius AB. Each curved side subtends π/3 at its own centre.

\[P=6 + 4 \pi\]

(b)

Take two sectors of angle π/3, then subtract the equilateral triangle counted twice.

\[A=\frac{\pi r^2}{3}-\frac{\sqrt3r^2}{4}=- 9 \sqrt{3} + 12 \pi\]
questions.hint_html: Join A, B and C before identifying the sector angles.

marking_criteria.description_html: Identifies both central angles as π/3.
Adds two arcs and the straight base.
Subtracts the common equilateral triangle once.

questions.prompt_html:
ABC is equilateral with side \(4\) cm. Each side of a coin is the minor circular arc joining two vertices, centred at the opposite vertex.

questions.title: The lens between two equal circles
questions.prompt_html:
Two circles have radius \(4\) cm and centres P and Q separated by \(\frac{16}{3}\) cm. Their common region is shaded.

  1. Find the angle subtended by the common chord at each centre.

    [3]

  2. Find the overlap area and perimeter to 3 significant figures.

    [5]
questions.answer_html:
(a) \(2 \cos^{-1}{\left(\frac{2}{3} \right)}\) radians
(b) \(- \frac{64 \sqrt{5}}{9} + 32 \cos^{-1}{\left(\frac{2}{3} \right)}\) cm² (approximately \(11.0\) cm²). \(16 \cos^{-1}{\left(\frac{2}{3} \right)}\) cm (approximately \(13.5\) cm).
questions.solution_html:
(a)

The common chord bisects the line of centres at right angles. Half the chord angle has cosine PQ/(2r).

(b)

The lens contains two equal minor segments. Use two sector-minus-triangle areas. Its perimeter contains two minor arcs, with no straight chord.

\[A=- \frac{64 \sqrt{5}}{9} + 32 \cos^{-1}{\left(\frac{2}{3} \right)}\]\[P=16 \cos^{-1}{\left(\frac{2}{3} \right)}\]
questions.hint_html: Join the centres and the two intersection points.

marking_criteria.description_html: Uses the perpendicular bisector of the common chord.

questions.title: Two radii belonging to different circles
questions.prompt_html:
A circle with centre O and radius \(4\) cm passes through A and B. A second circle has centre A and radius \(6\) cm, passing through B and meeting ray AO at C beyond O. Use the upper intersection B.

  1. Find angle BAO in radians.

    [2]

  2. Find the area and perimeter bounded by OC, arc CB centred at A and BO, to 3 significant figures.

    [5]
questions.answer_html:
(a) \(\cos^{-1}{\left(\frac{3}{4} \right)}\) radians
(b) \(- 3 \sqrt{7} + 18 \cos^{-1}{\left(\frac{3}{4} \right)}\) cm² (approximately \(5.07\) cm²). \(6 \cos^{-1}{\left(\frac{3}{4} \right)} + 6\) cm (approximately \(10.3\) cm).
questions.solution_html:
(a)

In triangle AOB, AO = OB = r and AB = R. Bisect the base AB, or use the cosine rule, to obtain \(\cos\angle BAO=\frac{R}{2r}\).

(b)

Subtract triangle AOB from sector ACB. For the perimeter, OC + OB = (R − r) + r = R.

\[A=- 3 \sqrt{7} + 18 \cos^{-1}{\left(\frac{3}{4} \right)}\]\[P=6 \cos^{-1}{\left(\frac{3}{4} \right)} + 6\]
questions.hint_html: The angle needed for arc BC is at A, not O.

marking_criteria.description_html: Uses the sector centred at A with radius R.
Simplifies the straight boundary before adding the arc.

questions.prompt_html:
Two circles have radius \(5\) cm and centres O and C with \(OC=5\text{ cm}\). They meet at A and B. The shaded crescent is inside the circle centred at O and outside the circle centred at C.

The two centres and either intersection make an equilateral triangle. The retained arcs have angles 4π/3 about O and 2π/3 about C.

questions.title: Two arcs on the same side of one chord
questions.prompt_html:
A circle has centre O and radius \(4\) cm. Its points A and B subtend \(\frac{14}{5}\) radians at O. C is the midpoint of the major arc AB. A second circle, centred at C, passes through A and B. The lune is bounded by the two minor arcs AB, on the side of AB away from C.

  1. Find angle ACB and the larger radius R in terms of r.

    [3]

  2. Find the area and perimeter of the lune to 3 significant figures.

    [5]
questions.answer_html:
(a) \(\frac{7}{5}\) radians; \(R=2 \cos{\left(\frac{7}{10} \right)}r\)
(b) \(- 32 \left(\frac{7}{5} - \sin{\left(\frac{7}{5} \right)}\right) \cos^{2}{\left(\frac{7}{10} \right)} - 8 \sin{\left(\frac{14}{5} \right)} + \frac{112}{5}\) cm² (approximately \(12.0\) cm²). \(\frac{56 \cos{\left(\frac{7}{10} \right)}}{5} + \frac{56}{5}\) cm (approximately \(19.8\) cm).
questions.solution_html:
(a)

Write θ for angle AOB. The angle at C subtended by chord AB is half the central angle AOB. In triangle AOC, AO = OC = r. The cosine rule gives \(R=2r\cos(\frac\theta4)\).

(b)

The lune is the small-circle segment minus the segment of the larger circle, both lying to the right of chord AB. Their angles are θ and θ/2 respectively.

\[A=- \frac{112 \cos{\left(\frac{7}{5} \right)}}{5} + 16 \sin{\left(\frac{7}{5} \right)}\]\[P=\frac{56 \cos{\left(\frac{7}{10} \right)}}{5} + \frac{56}{5}\]
questions.hint_html: The two segments share the same straight chord, which cancels from the region boundary.

questions.title: A chord equal to the larger radius
questions.prompt_html:
A circle with centre O, radius \(4\) cm, passes through A, B and C. C is the midpoint of the major arc AB. A larger circle has centre C and passes through A and B. Its radius equals AB.

  1. Show that the larger radius is √3 r.

    [3]

  2. Find the exact area and perimeter inside the larger circle but outside the smaller one.

    [5]
questions.answer_html:
(a) \(4 \sqrt{3}\) cm
(b) \(8 \sqrt{3} + \frac{88 \pi}{3}\) cm²; \(\frac{16 \pi}{3} + \frac{20 \sqrt{3} \pi}{3}\) cm
questions.solution_html:
(a)

AB equals the larger radius, so it subtends π/3 at C. The same chord subtends 2π/3 at O, on the side away from C. Hence \(AB=2r\sin(\frac{\pi}{3})=\sqrt3r\).

(b)

The common lens contains a 4π/3 sector of the small circle and a π/3 sector of the large circle, minus two triangles. Its area is \((\frac{7\pi}{6}-\frac{\sqrt3}{2})r^2\). Subtract this from \(3\pi r^2\). The exposed large arc is 5π/3; the concave small-circle arc is 4π/3.

\[A=8 \sqrt{3} + \frac{88 \pi}{3}\]\[P=\frac{4 \pi \left(4 + 5 \sqrt{3}\right)}{3}\]
questions.hint_html: The requested area is larger-disc-only, not the smaller lune.

Relates the central angles using the circumference point C.
Finds the common lens using the correct major small-circle segment.
Subtracts that lens from the larger disc.

questions.title: A tangent between externally touching circles
questions.prompt_html:
Circles centred at A and B have radii \(4\) cm and \(7\) cm and touch externally at C. A tangent from B meets the smaller circle at D above AB. It crosses the larger circle at E between D and B.

  1. Find the tangent length BD and the angles CAD and CBE.

    [3]

  2. Find the perimeter and area bounded by arc CD of the small circle, DE and arc EC of the large circle, to 3 significant figures.

    [5]
questions.answer_html:
(a) \(\sqrt{105}\) cm; \(\cos^{-1}{\left(\frac{4}{11} \right)}\) radians; \(\sin^{-1}{\left(\frac{4}{11} \right)}\) radians
(b) \(-7 + 7 \sin^{-1}{\left(\frac{4}{11} \right)} + 4 \cos^{-1}{\left(\frac{4}{11} \right)} + \sqrt{105}\) cm (approximately \(10.6\) cm). \(- 8 \cos^{-1}{\left(\frac{4}{11} \right)} - \frac{49 \sin^{-1}{\left(\frac{4}{11} \right)}}{2} + 2 \sqrt{105}\) cm² (approximately \(1.79\) cm²).
questions.solution_html:
(a)

ACB is a straight line and AB = r + R. In right triangle ADB, \(BD=\sqrt{AB^2-r^2}\), \(\cos\angle CAD=\frac r{AB}\) and the angle at B is the complement.

(b)

DE = BD − R. The area is triangle ADB minus sector ACD minus sector BCE. The sectors have different radii and complementary angles.

\[P=-7 + 7 \sin^{-1}{\left(\frac{4}{11} \right)} + 4 \cos^{-1}{\left(\frac{4}{11} \right)} + \sqrt{105}\]\[A=- 8 \cos^{-1}{\left(\frac{4}{11} \right)} - \frac{49 \sin^{-1}{\left(\frac{4}{11} \right)}}{2} + 2 \sqrt{105}\]
questions.hint_html: The straight boundary DE is shorter than the full tangent BD.

questions.title: A rope around seven touching pipes
questions.prompt_html:
Seven equal circular pipes of radius \(4\) cm are packed with one at the centre and six around it, all neighbouring pipes touching. A thin taut rope follows the outer boundary.

  1. Find the angle of rope in contact with each outer pipe.

    [2]

  2. Find the exact rope length.

    [3]

  3. Find the exact area of the centre hexagon and of the complete region enclosed by the rope.

    [5]
questions.answer_html:
(a) \(\frac{\pi}{3}\) radians
(b) \(8 \pi + 48\) cm
(c) \(96 \sqrt{3}\) cm²; \(16 \pi + 96 \sqrt{3} + 192\) cm²
questions.solution_html:
(a)

The six outer centres form a regular hexagon. Each change of direction is its exterior angle, 2π/6.

(b)

Six straight tangent pieces each have length 2r. The six curved pieces together make one complete circumference.

\[L=8 \pi + 48\]

(c)

The centre hexagon is six equilateral triangles of side 2r. Around it are six rectangles with combined area 12r² and six sectors with combined area πr².

\[A=16 \pi + 96 \sqrt{3} + 192\]
questions.hint_html: The rope does not run around the circumference of each complete pipe.

marking_criteria.description_html: Uses the regular hexagon of centres.

questions.title: A major arc and two outward semicircles
questions.prompt_html:
B, D and F lie on a circle of radius \(4\) cm centred at O, with \(\angle BOD=\angle DOF=\theta=\frac{6}{5}\). The plate boundary is the major arc BF away from D and two semicircles on BD and DF, bulging away from O.

Angles are measured in radians.

  1. Find the plate area to 3 significant figures.

    [5]

  2. Instead, each semicircle has area \(2 \pi\) cm². Find the exact perimeter of the new plate.

    [4]
questions.answer_html:
(a) \(- \frac{96}{5} + 16 \sin{\left(\frac{6}{5} \right)} + 16 \pi \sin^{2}{\left(\frac{3}{5} \right)} + 16 \pi\) cm² (approximately \(62.0\) cm²).
(b) \(\frac{28 \pi}{3}\) cm
questions.solution_html:
(a)

Each added semicircle has radius \(\rho=r\sin(\frac{\theta}{2})\). The central part is the major sector plus triangles OBD and ODF; then add the two outward semicircles.

\[A=r^2(\pi-\theta+\sin\theta)+\pi\rho^2=- \frac{96}{5} + 16 \sin{\left(\frac{6}{5} \right)} + 16 \pi \sin^{2}{\left(\frac{3}{5} \right)} + 16 \pi\]

(b)

The semicircle radius is r/2. Thus \(\sin(\frac{\theta}{2})=\frac12\) and θ = π/3. The boundary is a 4π/3 outer arc plus two semicircles of radius r/2.
questions.hint_html: The small angle at O subtended by BF is 2θ, not θ.

questions.title: Reconstructing two circles from their common chord
questions.prompt_html:
Two distinct circles of radius \(4\) cm meet at A and B, where \(AB=\frac{32}{5}\text{ cm}\). Their centres are P and Q. The shaded region is the union of the two discs.

  1. Find the distance PQ exactly and the minor central angle subtended by AB.

    [3]

  2. Find the union area and its external perimeter to 3 significant figures.

    [5]
questions.answer_html:
(a) \(\frac{24}{5}\) cm; \(2 \cos^{-1}{\left(\frac{3}{5} \right)}\) radians
(b) \(- 32 \cos^{-1}{\left(\frac{3}{5} \right)} + \frac{384}{25} + 32 \pi\) cm² (approximately \(86.2\) cm²). \(- 16 \cos^{-1}{\left(\frac{3}{5} \right)} + 16 \pi\) cm (approximately \(35.4\) cm).
questions.solution_html:
(a)

Half the common chord and half the centre separation form a right triangle with hypotenuse r. Use the positive centre separation, then the half-angle cosine ratio.

(b)

The union area is two full discs minus their lens. The external perimeter uses two major arcs, each subtending \(2\pi-2u\). The common chord is internal.

\[A=- 32 \cos^{-1}{\left(\frac{3}{5} \right)} + \frac{384}{25} + 32 \pi\]\[P=- 16 \cos^{-1}{\left(\frac{3}{5} \right)} + 16 \pi\]
questions.hint_html: The lens is not the requested region, but it is useful for calculating the union.

marking_criteria.description_html: Uses both perpendicular bisectors of the common chord.
Computes the overlap as two minor segments.

Uses the two exposed major arcs.

questions.title: Designing a sector around a circular hole
questions.prompt_html:
A circular hole of radius r touches both straight sides and the outer arc of a sector of radius R. The half-angle is u, with \(0<u<\frac{\pi}{2}\). It is given that \(\frac Rr=1 + \sqrt{2}\) and the outer-sector perimeter is \(\left(8 + 8 \sqrt{2}\right) \left(\frac{\pi}{4} + 1\right)\) cm.

Angles are measured in radians.

  1. Find the half-angle u exactly.

    [3]

  2. Find both radii exactly using the given outer-sector perimeter.

    [3]

  3. Find the perimeter of all the remaining material and the percentage of the sector area which remains after the circular hole is cut out.

    [4]
questions.answer_html:
(a) \(\frac{\pi}{4}\) radians
(b) \(4\) cm; \(4 + 4 \sqrt{2}\) cm
(c) \(8 \pi + \left(8 + 8 \sqrt{2}\right) \left(\frac{\pi}{4} + 1\right)\) cm; \(31.4\) %
questions.solution_html:
(a)

Internal tangency gives OC = R − r. The perpendicular radius to a straight side gives \(\sin u=\frac r{R-r}=\frac{1}{\frac Rr-1}\). Use \(0<u<\frac{\pi}{2}\).

(b)

The perimeter is \(P=2R+2Ru\). Recover R, then divide by the given ratio \frac Rr.

(c)

The hole adds its complete circumference to the material boundary. The remaining area is \(R^2u-\pi r^2\). Divide by the original sector area R²u before multiplying by 100.

\[P_{material}=8 \pi + 2 \left(1 + \sqrt{2}\right) \left(\pi + 4\right)\]
questions.hint_html: The requested final perimeter includes the boundary of the hole.

marking_criteria.description_html: Relates centre distance to the difference of radii.
Uses the perpendicular distance to a sector side.
Finds R, then r from their ratio.
Includes the entire inner circumference in addition to the outer boundary.
Uses remaining area divided by the original sector area.

questions.title: One rope, two different pipe bundles
questions.prompt_html:
Three equal circular pipes of radius \(4\) cm touch pairwise, with centres forming an equilateral triangle. A thin taut rope holds them together. In parts (b) and (c), the same rope is reused for a seven-pipe bundle of a different pipe radius. You may use: a seven-pipe centre hexagon has perimeter 12s and area \(6\sqrt3s^2\).

Angles are measured in radians.

  1. Find the exact rope length around the three-pipe bundle.

    [3]

  2. The same rope is used around seven equal touching pipes arranged as one central pipe and six outer pipes. Find their radius and the difference in enclosed areas, stating which bundle encloses more.

    [5]

  3. Which bundle has the greater proportion of its enclosed region occupied by pipe cross-sections? Give both percentages.

    [3]
questions.answer_html:
(a) \(24 + 8 \pi\) cm
(b) \(\frac{24 + 8 \pi}{2 \pi + 12}\) cm; seven-pipe area exceeds three-pipe area by \(-96 - 16 \pi - 16 \sqrt{3} + \frac{\left(24 + 8 \pi\right)^{2} \left(\pi + 6 \sqrt{3} + 12\right)}{\left(2 \pi + 12\right)^{2}}\) cm² (approximately \(10.4\) cm²).
(c) \(three: 86.7\%,\quad seven: 86.1\%\); the three-pipe bundle has the greater proportion.
questions.solution_html:
(a)

The three centre-to-centre sides have length 2r, giving 6r of straight rope. The three contact arcs each turn through 2π/3, giving a complete 2πr of curved rope.

(b)

For seven pipes \(L=(12+2\pi)s\), so \(s=\frac{24 + 8 \pi}{2 \pi + 12}\). The three-pipe area is \((\sqrt3+6+\pi)r^2\); the seven-pipe area is \((6\sqrt3+12+\pi)s^2\). These formulae include centre polygons, straight side strips and the combined corner sectors. Subtract after rescaling.

(c)

Divide the total pipe-disc area by the complete rope-enclosed area in each model. The squared radius cancels, so the comparison does not depend on the common rope length.
questions.hint_html: For any of these convex bundles, the curved contact pieces together turn through 2π.

marking_criteria.description_html: Uses three exterior contact angles totalling 2π.
Uses the seven-pipe rope equation with a new radius.
Includes polygon, strips and sectors for the three-pipe area.
Uses pipe-disc area over the whole enclosed area.

questions.title: One rope, two different pipe bundles
questions.prompt_html:
Three equal circular pipes of radius \(6\) cm touch pairwise, with centres forming an equilateral triangle. A thin taut rope holds them together. In parts (b) and (c), the same rope is reused for a seven-pipe bundle of a different pipe radius. You may use: a seven-pipe centre hexagon has perimeter 12s and area \(6\sqrt3s^2\).

Angles are measured in radians.

  1. Find the exact rope length around the three-pipe bundle.

    [3]

  2. The same rope is used around seven equal touching pipes arranged as one central pipe and six outer pipes. Find their radius and the difference in enclosed areas, stating which bundle encloses more.

    [5]

  3. Which bundle has the greater proportion of its enclosed region occupied by pipe cross-sections? Give both percentages.

    [3]
questions.answer_html:
(a) \(36 + 12 \pi\) cm
(b) \(\frac{36 + 12 \pi}{2 \pi + 12}\) cm; seven-pipe area exceeds three-pipe area by \(-216 - 36 \pi - 36 \sqrt{3} + \frac{\left(36 + 12 \pi\right)^{2} \left(\pi + 6 \sqrt{3} + 12\right)}{\left(2 \pi + 12\right)^{2}}\) cm² (approximately \(23.4\) cm²).
(c) \(three: 86.7\%,\quad seven: 86.1\%\); the three-pipe bundle has the greater proportion.
questions.solution_html:
(a)

The three centre-to-centre sides have length 2r, giving 6r of straight rope. The three contact arcs each turn through 2π/3, giving a complete 2πr of curved rope.

(b)

For seven pipes \(L=(12+2\pi)s\), so \(s=\frac{36 + 12 \pi}{2 \pi + 12}\). The three-pipe area is \((\sqrt3+6+\pi)r^2\); the seven-pipe area is \((6\sqrt3+12+\pi)s^2\). These formulae include centre polygons, straight side strips and the combined corner sectors. Subtract after rescaling.

(c)

Divide the total pipe-disc area by the complete rope-enclosed area in each model. The squared radius cancels, so the comparison does not depend on the common rope length.
questions.hint_html: For any of these convex bundles, the curved contact pieces together turn through 2π.
